content:
ISLAMABAD – Pakistan has issued a flood alert after India released water from the Salal Dam for the 11th consecutive time, with officials expecting a water surge of around 90,000 cusecs to reach Pakistan.

Reports said monitoring of river conditions has been increased as authorities prepare for the expected water flow.

Most rivers across the country are currently experiencing normal water levels; however, low to medium-level flooding continues at several locations along the Indus River.

Moderate flooding remains at Sukkur Barrage on the Indus River, while low-level flood conditions have been reported at the Kalabagh, Chashma, and Guddu barrages. Low-level flooding has also been recorded at Head Balloki on the Ravi River.

Meanwhile, water flows at key points along the Jhelum, Chenab, Sutlej, Ravi, and Kabul rivers remain within normal ranges. A decrease in water flow has been recorded at Chacharan Sharif and Benazir Bridge, where the discharge was reported at 218,978 cusecs.

Water levels at major reservoirs have also increased. The water level at Tarbela Dam has reached 1,539 feet, with the dam filled to around 89 percent of its capacity, similar to the level recorded last year.

Mangla Dam’s water level has crossed 1,196 feet, with the reservoir currently around 57 percent full.

Relevant authorities have directed district administrations and rescue agencies to remain alert while closely monitoring river conditions and vulnerable low-lying areas.
title: Pakistan issues flood alert after Indian releases water from Salal Dam for 11th time

content:
ISLAMABAD – Pakistan issued fresh flood alert after India released 90,000 cusecs of water from the Salal Dam for the 11th consecutive time. While most rivers remain within normal limits, the swelling Indus has once again put vulnerable communities on edge, with authorities racing to monitor rising water levels and prepare for any further surge.

Data shows 90,000 cusecs of additional water released from India are expected to enter Pakistan, raising fears of worsening flood conditions in vulnerable downstream areas. The latest influx has already begun impacting Sindh, where floodwaters from the Indus River have inundated villages near Sehwan, forcing authorities to closely monitor the evolving situation. Emergency agencies and district administrations have been placed on high alert as water continues to move downstream.

Flood Forecasting Division data shows that while most of Pakistan’s river network remains within normal operating conditions, the Indus River is experiencing elevated flows at several strategic control points. At Kalabagh, inflows reached 333,703 cusecs, while Chashma Barrage recorded 272,903 cusecs. Guddu Barrage received 334,637 cusecs, and Sukkur Barrage, registered the highest inflow at 369,534 cusecs, reflecting sustained pressure across the Indus basin.

Flood Situation

Official hydrological observations classify Kalabagh, Chashma, Guddu, and Sukkur under low flood conditions, while Taunsa and Kotri continue to operate within normal limits.

Floodwaters have submerged low-lying villages around Sehwan, underscoring the growing humanitarian concerns if river levels continue to rise. Authorities have urged residents living along vulnerable riverbanks to remain vigilant as rescue teams prepare for possible evacuations.

Officials are maintaining continuous surveillance over embankments and flood-prone settlements to minimize potential losses should the situation deteriorate further. The incoming flows have also pushed water levels higher at Pakistan’s two largest reservoirs.

Tarbela Dam has risen to 1,539.54 feet, just over 10 feet below its maximum conservation level of 1,550 feet, and is now approximately 89% full, matching storage levels recorded during the same period last year. The reservoir received 234,000 cusecs while releasing 158,400 cusecs, indicating continued water accumulation.

Meanwhile, Mangla Dam has climbed to 1,197.2 feet, with storage reaching 57% capacity. The reservoir recorded an inflow of 60,000 cusecs against an outflow of only 7,000 cusecs, reflecting ongoing conservation of water.
